title: I Want to End This Love Game
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Childhood friends Yukiya Asagi and Miku Sakura have played the 'Love Game' since they were small: each says 'I love you' and whoever gets flustered loses. Now in high school, both have truly fallen for each other but refuse to admit it. Yukiya sheds his quiet-nerd image and borrows moves from Miku's favorite shojo manga to win her over.
life_message: Honesty about your feelings takes more courage than winning, and is worth more.

content.note: Teen romantic teasing, wall-pins and near-confessions; MangaDex rates it safe.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Losing face in the game matters to both, but stakes are playful embarrassment, never insult demanding answer.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Teens shape their own romance and image; school rules barely feature.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Childhood-friend bond, close to family, is the core loyalty; wider community secondary.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Yukiya and Miku are equals and rivals; no rank governs them.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Modern school life guided by pop-culture scripts, not custom or faith.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Yukiya's glow-up and both teens' feelings are the point; no material worries.

folkways.japan: Fear of losing face and indirect confession reflect Japanese norms of reserve; the kabedon move comes from shojo manga convention.

delivery.evidence: No review consulted on delivery; summaries show the message carried by plot and character choices (to verify).
delivery.note: The sources say little about delivery, so the default reading is that the message rides on the story's events.

winners_losers: Both players are meant to win by losing the game; pride and pretense are the only losers. Sympathy goes to sincerity.
